subject: english-literature
title: A-Text vs B-Text: The Textual Problem of Faustus
welcome_lead: Confront the most notorious textual problem in Renaissance drama and analyse how the A-text (1604) and B-text (1616) Faustus differ.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on the A-text and B-text of Marlowe's Doctor Faustus: textual variants and critical consequences.
final_note: There are at least two Doctor Faustuses. Choose your text consciously — the differences matter for what kind of tragedy you describe.

concepts.def: Quarto published 1604; shorter (around 1,500 lines), often considered closer to Marlowe's autograph by editors like Bevington & Rasmussen.
Quarto published 1616; longer (around 2,100 lines), includes added comic scenes likely written by Samuel Rowley and William Birde in 1602.
Philip Henslowe records a 1602 payment of £4 to Birde and Rowley for additions to Faustus; documentary basis for B-text additions.
David Bevington and Eric Rasmussen's Revels parallel-text edition (1993) sets A and B side by side and remains the scholarly standard.
Robin and Rafe (A) / Robin and Dick (B) parody Faustus's magic; the B-text expands these scenes, generating critical debate about tonal coherence.
Both texts end with the Chorus's 'Cut is the branch'; but the B-text adds a final scene with the scholars discovering Faustus's mangled limbs.

walkthroughs.body_html: First: the B-text adds 676 lines, mostly comic scenes at the papal court and the imperial court. Second: the B-text gives Faustus's final monologue minor verbal changes ('Ugly hell, gape not!' becomes 'Ugly hell, gape not, come not, Lucifer!'). Third: only the B-text contains the discovery scene where the scholars find Faustus's dismembered body. Editorial choice shapes interpretation: A presents a more austere, tragic Faustus; B emphasises grotesque physical damnation.

Philip Henslowe's diary records, on 22 November 1602, payment of £4 to William Birde and Samuel Rowley 'for ther adicyones in docter fostes'. This is concrete documentary evidence that the B-text's additions postdate Marlowe (d. 1593) by nearly a decade. Editors disagree about how much of the additional material is theirs. Knowing this provenance lets AO3 responses discuss authorship and collaboration with precision.

walkthroughs.h2: Which Faustus on the Examiner's Desk?
walkthroughs.body_html: specifies which edition is set; most contemporary teaching uses the A-text via the Bevington & Rasmussen edition or the New Mermaids/Norton. Critics like Leah Marcus argue the two texts represent different theological dramas: the A-text is more sceptical, the B-text more orthodox. AO5 responses gain credit for noting which text they are reading and what interpretive consequences follow.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a metaphor and a simile?
options: Metaphors are short and similes are long.
A soliloquy is when characters argue with each other.
Metaphors are true and similes are false.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states one thing IS another, making an implicit comparison without those connectives.
